text: Lesson one turned a vague request into a specific requirement. Now, before opening SQL Server Management Studio at all, we translate that requirement into a plan — in plain English, naming tables and joins before writing a single line of real SQL.

Carraway Supply runs on AdventureWorks2012, and this report needs exactly four tables, each with one job. SalesOrderDetail holds the dollar amounts — the line totals. SalesOrderHeader holds the order date and which territory the order belongs to. Product holds the product line. And SalesTerritory turns a territory ID into a readable region name.

Written as a plan, it reads like this: start at SalesOrderDetail, join up to SalesOrderHeader on SalesOrderID, join sideways to Product on ProductID, and join from the header's territory ID over to SalesTerritory. Filter where the order date falls in the current quarter, and group by territory name and product line. Every join key gets named before any real SQL exists — if you can't name the join key in plain English, you're not ready to write the join yet.

Notice the plan starts at the detail table, not the header. The number we're summing, LineTotal, lives on SalesOrderDetail, one row per line item. An order with three products makes three detail rows but only one header row. Starting from the header and joining outward is a classic way to accidentally double-count order totals — starting from detail avoids that trap entirely.

Two more decisions, still in plain English before any SQL. The filter: order date falls within the current quarter. The grouping: one output row per territory and product line combination together — a group is the pairing, not either column alone, exactly like multi-column GROUP BY always works.
That's the plan — four tables, three join keys, one filter, one grouping. Next lesson, we turn every piece of this plan into real, runnable T-SQL against AdventureWorks2012.
